column2: A wine merchant's son who served as page, soldier, diplomat and customs official and wrote The Canterbury Tales in English.
Chaucer's choice to write in English, in the dialect that became the national standard, made later poets treat him as the model of the vernacular.
The unnamed pilgrim who meets the company at the Tabard and describes each pilgrim with seemingly naive admiration, leaving the irony for readers.
The large, bold landlord of the Tabard, drawn from a real man, who proposes the tale-telling game and serves as its "governour" and judge.
The archbishop of Canterbury murdered in his cathedral, the "holy blissful martyr" whose shrine the pilgrims seek.
An ideal, "very, perfect, gentle knight" who loved chivalry, truth and honor, fought crusades across Christendom and heathendom, and rides in a rust-stained tunic straight from his voyage.
The Knight's twenty-year-old son, a curly-haired lover embroidered like a meadow, who sings all day and sleeps no more than a nightingale.
The Knight's servant, a forester in green carrying peacock arrows, a bow and a silver St. Christopher.
The head of a convent who imitates court manners, sings through her nose, speaks the French of Stratford at the Bowe, weeps over a trapped mouse and wears a brooch reading "Amor vincit omnia."
A fat, bald, hunting outrider who rejects the old strict Rule of Saint Benedict and Saint Maure, keeps greyhounds and fine horses, and loves a roast swan.
A merry limitour who sells easy penance for gifts, knows every tavern better than lepers or beggars, and is called the best beggar in his house.
A forked-bearded trader who speaks solemnly of his profits and hides that he is in debt.
A lean, threadbare student of logic who would rather have twenty books of Aristotle than rich robes and who gladly learns and gladly teaches.
A gap-toothed, somewhat deaf cloth-maker from beside Bath who has had five husbands at the church door, travels to many shrines and knows "the olde dance" of love.
A poor but holy parish priest who visits his far-flung flock on foot and "first he wrought, and afterward he taught."
The Parson's brother, a true laborer who loves God and his neighbor, threshes and digs for the poor without pay, and pays his tithes fully.
A stout, red-bearded wrestler with a wart on his nose who steals corn, has a "thumb of gold," and plays the bagpipe to lead the pilgrims out of town.
A slender, choleric estate manager and carpenter who cheats his lord and takes the Miller's Tale as a personal attack.
A fire-red-faced officer of the church courts who takes bribes and tells sinners "Purse is the Archedeacon's helle."
A beardless, goat-voiced seller of pardons "from Rome all hot" who uses fake relics to get more money in a day than a poor parson gets in two months.
The Church Father whose attack on Jovinian supplied the antifeminist authorities the Wife argues against.
A monk who apparently presented marriage as a positive good, known only through Jerome's attack on him.
The apostle whose letters the Wife cites, arguing he only counseled virginity and gave wives power over husbands' bodies.
The Wife's fifth husband, a twenty-year-old former Oxford clerk who reads her antifeminist tales nightly until their fight ends with him burning the book.
The Wife's close friend in town, with whom Jankin boarded and to whom the Wife told all her husband's secrets.
The "foule cherl" who beat his wife to death with a staff for drinking wine, whose example the Wife says could not have stopped her.

column1: The knight in the Wife's Tale
column2: A young knight of Arthur's court who rapes a maiden, must learn what women most desire to save his life, and is forced to marry the old wife.
The foul old woman who gives the knight the answer in return for his pledge, marries him, lectures him on gentilesse, and becomes fair and good once given mastery.

column1: The queen in the Wife's Tale
column2: Arthur's queen, who with other ladies pleads for the knight's life and then sets him the question of what women most desire.
Midas hid his ass's ears from all but his wife, who could not keep the secret and whispered it into a marsh, the Wife's proof that women cannot hide a secret.
The Italian poet whom the old wife cites to prove that prowess and gentilesse come from God, not ancestry.
The Italian writer whose Decameron is the most famous frame tale besides Chaucer's and whose works supplied plots for the Knight's Tale and Troilus.
Chaucer's contemporary whose Lover's Confession uses a frame in which a single speaker tells all the stories.
The man who introduced printing to England and twice printed The Canterbury Tales.
